title: Inferior Visual Field Defects: A Clinical Diagnostic Atlas
summary: Inferior visual field loss is a critical localizing sign in neuro-ophthalmology, often pointing to superior retinal or post-chiasmal pathway pathology. This guide navigates the topographic mapping of the visual system to localize lesions based on perimetric findings.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Emergent Causes
content: Sudden onset altitudinal defect: Rule out Arteritic AION (GCA) with ESR/CRP/PLT.
Transient loss: Rule out amaurosis fugax or impending central retinal artery occlusion.
Bilateral inferior defects: Evaluate for pituitary mass causing superior chiasmal compression.
Progressive defects with headache: Mandatory neuroimaging (MRI Brain/Orbits with contrast).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Confrontation field testing to confirm defect pattern.
Step 2: Automated Perimetry (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2) to quantify density/scotoma depth.
Step 3: Slit-lamp exam with 90D/78D lens to inspect superior retina and optic nerve head.
Step 4: OCT (RNFL) to detect nerve fiber layer thinning corresponding to the defect.
Step 5: Neuroimaging (MRI) if post-chiasmal lesion is suspected (homonymous pattern).

content.explanation: Parietal = Inferior (field defect); Temporal = Superior (field defect).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Altitudinal defects that respect the horizontal meridian are typically pre-chiasmal (optic nerve).
Homonymous defects that respect the vertical meridian are post-chiasmal (chiasm/tracts/radiation/cortex).
In a pituitary adenoma, the compression is from below, causing a SUPERIOR field defect first; however, anatomical variations can present as inferior.
Always perform gonioscopy in glaucoma patients with inferior defects to rule out angle-closure history.
